newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: PMP shares slide as News exits.
newsitem.headline: PMP shares slide as News exits.

text.p: Shares in multimedia publisher PMP Communications Ltd sank nearly 14 percent to A$3.15 in early trade on Wednesday after News Corporation Ltd announced the sale of its 40.33 percent stake.
The sale was specialled in a line of 101.6 million shares through Were Stockbroking at a price of A$3.20 per share.

Brokers said concerns about an overhang from the large block of shares had shunted the price lower and uncertainty remained about whether Were had actually allocated the full 101.6 million shares to institutional investors.
Opinion among analysts was divided about whether News had sold cheaply or had chosen a good time to offload what was seen a relatively low-growth stock.

"They've gotten out cheap. It's an excellent deal for the institutions," said one media analyst. "There's no way you would have got the sort of parcels the insitutions have got by buying on market at A$3.20 a share," he said.

Some analysts and brokers wondered whether recent fruitless speculation about a A$4.00 a share takeover bid by a U.S. group had been linked to the sale at A$3.20, having helped boost it to Tuesday's A$3.65 close from its three month low of A$3.29 on June 12.
The sale price was well above the 1997 low of A$2.98 reached on April 3.
Some saw it as good news for both News and PMP, removing an unstable shareholder from PMP's board room and putting cash in News' accounts to lower its gearing and reassure nervous ratings agencies.
"It's a positive for PacMag in the medium term and a positive for News Corp," said another analyst.
ANZ Investment Banking media analyst Bob Peters said PMP had only moderate growth prospects, particularly since its acquisition of the poorly performed Shomega multi-media unit.
"It's not in the fast growth electronic media sector and consequently Pacific Magazines is a low growth stock and had to be priced on yield to get the stock away," Peters said.
"From News' point of view it's focusing on the high growth areas," he said.

"There was a need to satisfy the financial community's concerns in terms of gearing and so it's been disposing of some of its peripheral assets like Australian Newsprint Mill and Pacific Magazines locally, and probably more odds and sods will follow."

"Its pay television programming production and distribution is a fastgrowing but avarice beast and requires on-going funding, so a decision has been made to get into the growth areas of the future and get out of the some of the traditional media sectors."
Peters said News may now look to exit some of its low growth publishing and print interests in the United States.
Brokers said Were may struggle to get rid of the stock.
"It hasn't been a great story. Few people like the stock," said Neil Franklin, a broker at HSBC James Capel.
Franklin said the sale price of A$3.20 was below the A$3.40 issue price when the company floated in 1992.
He said PMP, formerly Pacific Magazines, forecast earnings per share (EPS) of 29.9 cents in the 1992/93 year when it floated.
"But our forecasts they won't be making that by 1999," he said.
PMP reported 12.2 cents EPS in the first half of 1996/97 and has since forecast full year pre-tax earnings would be 15 to 20 percent below the A$90.38 million reported in the year to June 30 1996.
-- Bernard Hickey 61-2 9373-1812
